facts.claim: Shazam lists 'Both Sides Of The Moon' by Celeste & Gotts Street Park as released on 29 January 2021 by Polydor Records on the album Not Your Muse (Deluxe).
The track first appeared as a single on 28 September 2018 on Atlas Artists / Polydor Records, as 'Both Sides of the Moon (Live)'.
It was written by Celeste and Gotts Street Park and produced by Josh Crocker.

Credits include Josh Crocker on bass, organ and piano, and as mixer. Gordon Nicholl plays drums, Joe Harris guitar and Tom Henry keyboards. Todd Simon plays flugelhorn and French horn, and Juliane Gralle bass trombone. Crocker and Simon arranged the horns.
Tim Montague was assistant recording engineer and John Davis was mastering engineer. Qobuz also credits Crocker with recording engineering and string arrangement.

Gotts Street Park say they wrote 'Both Sides of the Moon' and 'Lately' with Celeste in two days. The session was at Josh Crocker's basement setup in Leeds, after a London writing session where she was still almost unknown and wanted to jam with a live band.
Gotts Street Park formed in Leeds. Tom and Joe met at Leeds College of Music on a jazz course, and they later met Josh through the Leeds music scene.
The song's lyrics are about doubt and betrayal in a relationship, and use the moon and the tide as imagery.

The song comes from Celeste's earlier 2018–19 'Lately' period. It was added to the deluxe edition of her debut album Not Your Muse, which came out on 29 January 2021 through Both Sides and Polydor and went to number one on the UK Albums Chart.
Celeste (Celeste Epiphany Waite) was born in the US in 1994 and raised in Brighton. She won the BBC Sound of 2020 poll and the BRITs Rising Star award.

research.lineage: A live-band, vintage-leaning jazz-soul song made with Leeds jazz-trained musicians, in the British soul revival that Celeste later brought to a wide audience.

draft:
The detail that cracks **Both Sides Of The Moon** open is a smell. "I smelled the cinnamon, how could I depend?" Celeste sings, and the whole song turns on that one sensory clue: a scent that isn't hers, picked up on someone who came home. It's an oddly domestic way to discover betrayal, and that's why it lands. Nobody in this song finds a letter or catches a lie outright. The narrator just knows, the way you know, and then has to live inside the knowing.

What makes the lyric hard to shake is how many feelings it refuses to sort out. Suspicion has already "proved me right," yet the next breath is "Did I deserve it?", self-blame arriving right on the heels of being wronged. Later she's "pacing back with him," pain in the chest, still telling herself "I'm hoping they're just friends." That line is the saddest one in the song because the narrator doesn't believe it and says it anyway. The pronouns slip, too: "he" in one line, "you" in the next, as if she can't decide whether to talk about this person or to them. The chorus explains why she can't leave. "And the moon is a slave to the tides" flips the usual physics, making the moon the thing being pulled, and that's exactly how this love feels from the inside: something that should be in charge, dragged around by forces it can't refuse. "Both sides" works twice over, seeing the bright face and the dark one, and being stuck arguing both cases in your own head.

The music doesn't dramatize any of this, which is the point. A slow, laid-back groove sits under a tight, dry snare. The bass walks simply, warm sustained piano chords hang in the air, and a clean electric guitar shimmers in arpeggios. Celeste's voice is breathy with a little rasp at the edges, delivered smooth and sustained, so the hurt comes out composed. There's a lot of room around every instrument.

That roominess has a source. Gotts Street Park, a Leeds band whose members met on a jazz course at Leeds College of Music, say they wrote this and "Lately" with Celeste in two days in Josh Crocker's basement setup in Leeds, after she'd asked to jam with a live band while still almost unknown. Crocker produced and played bass, organ and piano; Gordon Nicholl drums, Joe Harris guitar, Tom Henry keys, with horns from Todd Simon and Juliane Gralle. It's British jazz-soul made by players, released first as a live single in 2018, then folded into the deluxe edition of *Not Your Muse*, the album that took Celeste to number one.

The song lets you sit inside the moment you already know the truth and still can't make yourself stop hoping.
